h1: Market research for a new wine brand
title: Market Research for a New Wine Brand | Craft Beer School
desc: How to research a wine market before launch: who buys, at what price, from where, plus shelf checks, buyer interviews and tasting panels.
teaser: Before you make a bottle, find out who will buy it, where they shop and what they pay.
standfirst: Market research tells you whether the wine you want to make is a wine anyone wants to buy. Here is a practical way to gather evidence on a small budget.
sections:
Good research starts with decisions. What will you make, for whom, at what price and through which channel? Write down the questions the research should answer. Common ones are: who buys wine like this, how often, where and at what price? Why would they pick a new label over a known one?

Do not collect data for its own sake. Each answer should change something you will do.

Start with what already exists: import and domestic wine lists, shop and restaurant menus, online shops, trade reports, regulator publications and news. Use sources you can name. Be careful with market-size claims in press releases, since they often rest on thin evidence. Where a figure matters to your plan, find the original source or leave it out and use your own numbers.

Look at competitors one by one. Note their range, prices, bottle design, story and distribution.

Check the dates on everything you read. A price list from two years ago is history. Keep a simple sheet with the source, date and what you used it for, so a lender or partner can see where each fact came from.

Go to shops and restaurants where you hope to sell. Record, for each wine in your style and price band, the name, producer, origin, price, bottle, closure, position on the shelf and number of facings. Photograph the shelf if the shop allows. Repeat on different days and in different areas. An hour in ten shops gives a sharp picture of what sits where and at what price. Our guide on pricing wine shows how to use it.

Take a note of what is missing. A gap in style or price on the shelf can be an opening or a warning that nobody buys it.

Interview shop buyers, restaurant managers, sommeliers and distributors. Ask open questions: what sells, what does not, what do customers ask for, what margin do you need and what annoys you about suppliers? Listen more than you talk. Ask for a reaction to your concept, not praise.

Record answers and look for patterns across ten or more conversations. One loud opinion is an opinion. Five similar ones are evidence.

Ask about the buying cycle. When do shops list new wines, who decides and what do they need to see before a first order? Buyers often have a quiet period before big seasons, so timing your visit matters. Ask what a good sample looks like and how long they give it before judging.

Run a small tasting panel. Pour your sample next to two or three competitor wines without labels. Ask people to rank them and say what they would pay. Use a mix of people who match your intended customer, not only friends. Keep the setting fair: same glasses, same temperature, same pour size. Responsible tasting rules apply, so offer water, allow spitting and never press anyone to drink.

A prototype bottle tells you more than a presentation. If you do not yet have wine, taste samples from a contract producer or similar styles.

A short survey can test price points and preferences with a wider group. Keep it brief, avoid leading questions and be wary of conclusions from a small or self-selected sample. Treat the results as a signal, not a forecast. For research with a larger sample or a structured design, a professional can run consumer surveys and retail audits.

Whatever you use, do not invent figures. If you only have thirty answers, say so.

If you survey, test the questions on five people first. Ask about behaviour, such as what wine they bought last, rather than intentions, such as what they would buy. Intentions are generous. Past behaviour is a better guide.

Summarise findings on one page: target customer, price band, channel, competitor gaps, the story that landed and what you will change. Feed the answers into your winery business plan and your cost per bottle. If the evidence says the wine does not fit the market, that is a cheap result. Finding out after the first vintage is not.

Set a rule before you start. For example: if fewer than half of the buyers we interview would stock the wine at our price, we change the price, the style or the channel. A rule written in advance stops you reading the results the way you hoped.
faqs: How much market research is enough?
Enough to change a decision. Ten shop audits, ten buyer interviews and one tasting panel can reveal a lot for a small brand.
Can I do market research myself?
Yes for the basics. A professional helps with larger samples and structured surveys.
What if no data exists for my market?
Build your own through audits, interviews and tastings. State the limits.
Yes, with real buyers and a blind comparison, since people say one thing and buy another.
